newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Thai, Korea banks in tough mkt.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Thai, Korea banks in tough mkt.

text.p: Thailand's Siam Commercial Bank and Korea Long Term Credit Bank braved the Asian debt markets on Tuesday with new floating rate certificate of deposit issues.

Siam Commercial's five-year US$100 million FRCD issue was priced at par to float at 35 basis points over the London Interbank Offered Rate. With fees, it pays an all-in return of 43 basis points to top-tier participants.
BA Asia is arranger and bookrunner for the transaction, while Nomura International (Hong Kong) and Sakura Finance Asia joined as arrangers.
Thailand's banks, which had been active participants in the debt markets, had all but stopped tapping offshore markets after investors turned skittish about the country's financial health.

Moody's Investors Service dealt Thailand a blow by downgrading its sovereign rating to A3 from A2. Moody's also cut the ratings of several banks, including Siam Commercial, which it cut to A3 from A2.

Standard and Poor's Corp also has downgraded a number of Thai banks but has maintained Thailand's sovereign rating at Single-A on the view that the country is strong enough to weather problems in its financial sector.
S&P cut Siam Commercial's foreign currency debt to BBB-plus from A-minus in March.
Siam Commercial launched a US$120 million FRCD due July 2001 last year to give 32 basis points all-in.
The certificates are now indicated with a spread of 41-42 basis points, close to the pricing offered on the new five-year paper.
Bankers said Siam Commercial had sought pricing similar to what it had achieved last year but apparently was convinced in the end that it would need to pay a wider spread to entice market demand.
"It's a groundbreaking deal after all the bad news from Thailand," said a manager at BA Asia, adding that banks considering the deal seemed satisfied with the pricing.
A syndicate manager at another bank said that while the pricing on Siam Commercial "was not very tight" investors were still concerned about Thai risk.
Korea Long-Term Credit Bank formally launched its 364-day FRCD via lead managers ABN Amro Hoare Govett and Sakura Finance Asia.
The certificates pay a margin of 35 basis points over LIBOR and, with fees, an all-in return of 43 basis points. Last June, Korea Long paid in the low 30s for a three-year floating rate note issue.
Bankers said the big move in pricing reflected concerns over South Korea's financial sector following defaults of major companies earlier this year. Some called the pricing generous.
"To attract investors, the Korean banks need to pay a bigger premium," noted one banker, who said that the Korea Long issue could become a new benchmark for Korea paper.
